title: Hemoglobinopathies & Marrow Failure
summary: Inherited hemoglobin diseases and conditions where the marrow or complement system turns against blood cells.

lessons.title: Sickle Cell Disease: From One Mutation to Polymerization

levels.kid:
Your red blood cells are like soft, squishy donuts. They carry oxygen all around your body. Inside each one is a special helper called **hemoglobin** that grabs onto oxygen.

In **sickle cell disease**, there is one tiny spelling mistake in the instructions for making hemoglobin. Just one letter is different!

When the hemoglobin lets go of its oxygen, the faulty kind sticks together into long, stiff strings, like spaghetti that hardens. Those strings bend the soft red cell into a curved shape, like a banana or a farmer's tool called a sickle.

Sickled cells are stiff and sticky. They can get stuck in tiny blood tubes, like a traffic jam. A child gets sickle cell disease when both parents pass on the changed instructions.
levels.hs:
**Sickle cell disease (SCD)** is an inherited blood disorder caused by a change in the gene for **beta-globin**, one of the protein chains that make up **hemoglobin**, the oxygen-carrying molecule inside red blood cells.

Normal adult hemoglobin (**HbA**) has two alpha and two beta chains. In sickle hemoglobin (**HbS**), a single DNA letter change swaps one amino acid: **glutamic acid** at position 6 of beta-globin becomes **valine**. Glutamic acid is charged and water-loving; valine is oily and water-avoiding.

That tiny change matters when hemoglobin releases oxygen. Deoxygenated HbS molecules stick to each other through the new valine patch and line up into long fibers, a process called **polymerization**. The fibers distort the red cell into a rigid sickle shape. Sickled cells:
- block small blood vessels
- break apart early (they live about 10-20 days instead of about 120)
- make blood vessel linings inflamed and sticky

SCD is **autosomal recessive**. A person with one HbS gene and one normal gene has **sickle cell trait** and is usually healthy. Two HbS genes (HbSS) cause the most common form, sickle cell anemia. If two carriers have a child, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of SCD.

The trait is common in people with ancestry from Africa, the Middle East and India because carriers are partly protected from severe **malaria**.
levels.college:
**Molecular lesion.** HbS results from a point mutation in **HBB** on chromosome 11: codon 6 GAG becomes GTG, giving **Glu6Val** (often written E6V; historically beta6 Glu-to-Val). Linus Pauling's 1949 electrophoresis study showed HbS moves differently in an electric field, making SCD the first "molecular disease." Vernon Ingram identified the single amino acid swap in 1956.

**Why deoxygenation matters.** On deoxygenation, hemoglobin shifts from the R (relaxed) to the T (tense) state. In T-state HbS, the surface beta6 valine fits into a hydrophobic pocket (formed by beta85 Phe and beta88 Leu) on a beta chain of a neighboring tetramer. This sticky contact lets molecules assemble into **14-stranded helical fibers** that align into bundles, stretching the cell.

**Key determinants of polymerization:**
- **HbS concentration**: rate depends on a very high power of concentration, so cell dehydration greatly speeds sickling
- **Degree of deoxygenation**: low oxygen, acidosis and high 2,3-BPG favor the T state
- **Delay time**: a lag before fibers form; if a cell gets back to the lungs first, it may escape sickling
- **Fetal hemoglobin (HbF)**: gamma chains do not join the polymer and dilute HbS

**Consequences.** Repeated sickling damages the membrane, causes potassium and water loss (via Gardos and KCl channels), and produces irreversibly sickled cells. Results include **hemolytic anemia** and **vaso-occlusion**.

**Genotypes.** HbSS (sickle cell anemia), HbSC (HbS plus HbC, Glu6Lys), and HbS/beta-thalassemia (beta0 severe, beta+ milder) are the main forms. **Sickle cell trait (HbAS)** contains about 35-40% HbS, too little to sickle under normal conditions.

**Diagnosis** uses hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC; many countries do newborn screening.
levels.phd:
**Fiber structure.** Electron microscopy and crystallography (Wishner and Love's HbS crystal structure; Dykes and colleagues' fiber reconstructions) define the polymer as 14 strands arranged as 7 double strands twisted into a helix about 21 nm in diameter. Within each double strand, the beta6 Val of one tetramer makes the **lateral contact** with the EF-corner acceptor pocket (beta85 Phe, beta88 Leu) of the next. Only one of the two beta6 valines per tetramer is used. Additional axial and interstrand contacts explain why some hemoglobin variants strengthen or weaken polymerization.

**Kinetics: double nucleation.** Eaton and Hofrichter showed polymerization follows a **double nucleation mechanism**. Homogeneous nucleation in solution is followed by heterogeneous nucleation on existing fiber surfaces, producing explosive autocatalytic growth after a **delay time**. The delay time is inversely proportional to roughly the 30th power of supersaturation, so tiny changes in intracellular HbS concentration have huge effects. Because most capillary transit takes about 1 second, the fraction of cells with delay times shorter than transit largely decides how much sickling happens in vivo. This explains several clinical observations:
- **HbF** (alpha2gamma2) and hybrid alpha2betaSgamma tetramers are excluded from the polymer, lengthening the delay time
- **Co-inherited alpha-thalassemia** lowers MCHC and reduces hemolysis
- **HbC** causes cell dehydration, raising HbS concentration in HbSC cells

**Membrane pathobiology.** Repeated polymer cycling activates **Psickle** (likely Piezo1-linked) cation entry, raising Ca2+, which opens the **Gardos channel** (KCNN4) and causes K+ and water loss. Phosphatidylserine exposure, oxidative damage from unstable HbS, and microvesicle release follow.

**Beyond the red cell.** Hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, which scavenges **nitric oxide** and releases heme (a danger signal activating TLR4). Adhesion of reticulocytes (VLA-4, Lu/BCAM), neutrophils and platelets to endothelium (P-selectin, VCAM-1) shows vaso-occlusion is a multicellular inflammatory event, not just a mechanical blockage.

**Evolutionary genetics.** HbS arose on several haplotype backgrounds (Benin, Bantu/CAR, Senegal, Cameroon, Arab-Indian), linked to differing HbF levels. Heterozygote protection against *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria is a textbook case of **balanced polymorphism**.
levels.expert:
**Therapies built on polymer biophysics.** Because the delay time is so sensitive, small shifts in intracellular conditions bring large benefits:
- **Hydroxyurea** induces HbF (partly through stress erythropoiesis and nitric oxide-related signaling), lowers neutrophil counts and reduces adhesion. Benefit is linked to the proportion of **F-cells**, not just total HbF.
- **Voxelotor** stabilized the oxygenated R state to inhibit polymerization. It was withdrawn worldwide in 2024 after post-marketing data showed more vaso-occlusive events and deaths, a warning that raising hemoglobin and left-shifting oxygen affinity does not guarantee clinical benefit.
- **Pyruvate kinase activators** (mitapivat, etavopivat) lower 2,3-BPG and raise ATP, aiming at both polymerization and membrane health. Phase 3 data are maturing.
- **Crizanlizumab** (anti-P-selectin) targets adhesion; the STAND trial did not confirm lower crisis rates, and regulatory status in Europe was revoked.

**Genetic therapies.** The **BCL11A** discovery (Orkin, Sankaran and colleagues) showed this repressor silences gamma-globin after birth. **Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy)**, approved in 2023, uses CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt the BCL11A erythroid enhancer in autologous stem cells, restoring HbF. **Lovotibeglogene autotemcel (Lyfgenia)** adds an anti-sickling beta-globin variant (betaA-T87Q) by lentivirus. Both require myeloablative busulfan conditioning, with infertility and cost as major barriers. Base editing to convert HbS toward the benign Makassar variant is in development.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.**
- After transfusion, electrophoresis is misleading; HbA from donor blood masks the genotype
- HbS/beta+ thalassemia can look like sickle trait; check MCV and HbA2
- Solubility ("sickledex") tests detect HbS but do not distinguish trait from disease and may be false-negative in infants with high HbF
- Newborn "FS" patterns need confirmation, as HbS/beta0 thalassemia can look identical

**Open questions.** Why patients with the same genotype vary so much remains incompletely explained: HbF, alpha-thalassemia and haplotype account for only part. Sickle cell trait carries small but real risks (renal medullary carcinoma, exertional rhabdomyolysis in extreme conditions, hyposthenuria), which make blanket athletic screening controversial. Global access is a huge issue: most affected births occur in sub-Saharan Africa, where newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis and hydroxyurea, not gene therapy, save the most lives.

keyPoints: SCD comes from a single HBB mutation: Glu6Val at beta-globin position 6
Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into 14-stranded fibers via a hydrophobic valine contact
Polymerization has a delay time hugely sensitive to HbS concentration
Fetal hemoglobin does not join the polymer and protects against sickling
SCD is autosomal recessive; sickle trait (HbAS) protects against malaria
Newer therapies target HbF (hydroxyurea, BCL11A gene editing) and polymer biology

test.q: Which amino acid change causes sickle hemoglobin?
choices: Glutamic acid to valine at beta-6
Valine to glutamic acid at alpha-6
Glutamic acid to lysine at beta-6
test.explain: HbS is Glu6Val in beta-globin. Glu6Lys at beta-6 is HbC, a different variant.

test.q: Under what condition does HbS polymerize?
test.explain: Deoxygenated (T-state) HbS exposes the contact that lets molecules stick together and form fibers.

test.q: Why does the valine substitution promote sticking?
choices: It creates a hydrophobic surface patch
It adds a negative charge to the surface
It forms a disulfide bond with cysteine
It blocks heme from holding iron
test.explain: Valine is hydrophobic and fits into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring tetramer, linking molecules into fibers.

test.q: What is the inheritance pattern of sickle cell disease?
test.explain: Two abnormal beta-globin genes are needed for disease; one copy gives sickle cell trait.

test.q: Two parents both have sickle cell trait. What is the chance a given child has SCD?
test.explain: Each parent passes HbS half the time, so the chance of inheriting two copies is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

test.q: Why does fetal hemoglobin reduce sickling?
choices: It makes red cells larger and floppier
It binds HbS and breaks it down
It raises the cell's level of 2,3-BPG
Its gamma chains are left out of the polymer
test.explain: HbF tetramers and hybrids do not join the fiber, diluting HbS and lengthening the delay time.

test.q: Red cell dehydration worsens sickling mainly because it:
choices: Converts HbF back into adult HbA
Lowers the oxygen level in plasma
test.explain: Polymerization depends on a very high power of HbS concentration, so losing water speeds fiber formation dramatically.

test.q: Why is sickle cell trait common in some regions?
test.explain: Heterozygote protection against falciparum malaria keeps the HbS gene common where malaria is or was widespread.

test.q: Who first showed HbS behaves differently using electrophoresis in 1949?
test.explain: Pauling's 1949 study made SCD the first molecular disease; Ingram later found the exact amino acid swap.

test.q: What is the name of the gene on chromosome 11 that is mutated in sickle cell disease?
test.explain: HBB encodes beta-globin; codon 6 GAG becomes GTG.

test.q: The lag before HbS fibers suddenly form is called the ___ time.
test.explain: If a cell returns to the lungs before its delay time ends, it may escape sickling.

test.q: A person with one HbS gene and one normal gene has sickle cell ___.
test.explain: Sickle cell trait (HbAS) is usually symptom-free because HbS is only about 35-40% of the hemoglobin.

kidTest.q: What job does hemoglobin do?
kidTest.explain: Hemoglobin grabs oxygen and carries it around the body.

kidTest.q: What shape do sickle cells become?
kidTest.explain: The stiff strings inside bend the cell into a curved sickle shape.

kidTest.q: How big is the change in the instructions?
kidTest.explain: Only one letter in the instructions is different.

kidTest.q: Why can sickled cells cause trouble?
choices: They get stuck in tiny tubes
kidTest.explain: Stiff, sticky cells jam tiny blood vessels like a traffic jam.

kidTest.q: The faulty hemoglobin sticks together into stiff s _ _ _ _ _ _ when it lets go of oxygen.
kidTest.explain: The hemoglobin lines up into long stiff strings, like hardened spaghetti.

advancedTest.q: The delay time varies with about the 30th power of supersaturation. What does this most directly predict?
choices: Oxygen level has little effect once HbS is present
Fetal hemoglobin speeds up fiber nucleation in red cells
Sickling rate rises in a straight line with HbS concentration
Small drops in HbS concentration can sharply reduce sickling
advancedTest.explain: Extreme concentration dependence means modest dilution (by HbF or rehydration) lengthens the delay time beyond capillary transit.

advancedTest.q: Why does HbSC disease sickle more than sickle trait, even though both have one normal-looking non-S allele?
choices: HbC lowers the amount of fetal hemoglobin
HbC dehydrates cells, raising HbS concentration
HbC makes the valine pocket more hydrophobic
HbC joins HbS fibers as a full partner
advancedTest.explain: HbC promotes cell dehydration, raising intracellular HbS concentration enough to polymerize, unlike HbA in trait.

advancedTest.q: What does the 2024 withdrawal of voxelotor most strongly suggest?
choices: HbF induction is harmful in most adults
Gene therapy has largely replaced drug therapy
Polymerization plays little part in sickle cell disease
Raising hemoglobin is not proof of clinical benefit
advancedTest.explain: Voxelotor raised hemoglobin by stabilizing the R state, but post-marketing data showed more crises and deaths, so a lab marker did not equal patient benefit.

advancedTest.q: Why does Casgevy target the erythroid enhancer of BCL11A rather than the whole gene?
choices: To lower 2,3-BPG levels in red cells
To add a new anti-sickling beta-globin gene
To restore HbF while sparing other cell types
To fix the Glu6Val codon directly in HBB
advancedTest.explain: BCL11A represses gamma-globin in red cell precursors; disrupting only its erythroid enhancer raises HbF without affecting BCL11A roles in other lineages.

lessons.title: Sickle Cell Complications: Crises, Stroke & Organ Damage

levels.kid:
In sickle cell disease, some red blood cells bend into a curved shape, like a banana or a farmer's sickle. Healthy red cells are soft and round, so they slide easily through tiny blood tubes.

The curved cells are stiff and sticky. They can get stuck, like a traffic jam on a narrow road. When blood can't get through, that part of the body doesn't get enough oxygen, and it hurts a lot. Doctors call this a **pain crisis**.

Traffic jams can happen in the lungs, the brain, or the spleen, which is a blood filter in your belly. So doctors check kids with sickle cell often. They use a special sound scan of the head to spot brain blood vessels that might get blocked, and they act early to keep the brain safe.
levels.hs:
**Sickle cell disease (SCD)** is caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene. When oxygen levels drop, the abnormal hemoglobin (HbS) clumps into long fibers that deform red cells into stiff sickles. Most complications come from two problems:
- **Vaso-occlusion**: sickled, sticky cells block small blood vessels, starving tissue of oxygen (**ischemia**).
- **Hemolysis**: sickled cells break apart early, causing anemia and releasing free hemoglobin into the blood.

Major complications include:
- **Vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)**: sudden, severe pain, often in bones, back, or chest. It is the most common reason patients go to the hospital.
- **Acute chest syndrome (ACS)**: a new lung infiltrate on X-ray plus fever or breathing symptoms. It is a leading cause of death in SCD.
- **Stroke**: blockage of large brain arteries, most common in children.
- **Splenic sequestration**: blood suddenly pools in the spleen, causing a dangerous drop in hemoglobin in young children.
- **Infection**: repeated damage destroys the spleen (**autosplenectomy**), so children are vulnerable to bacteria like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*.

Example: a 7-year-old with SCD gets a **transcranial Doppler (TCD)** ultrasound each year. If blood flows abnormally fast in a brain artery, the narrowing means high stroke risk. Regular transfusions can then cut that risk dramatically.
levels.college:
SCD complications fall into two overlapping categories, with different patients leaning toward one or the other.

**Vaso-occlusive phenotype** (higher hemoglobin, higher blood viscosity): pain crises, acute chest syndrome, avascular necrosis.

**Hemolytic phenotype** (lower hemoglobin, high LDH): pulmonary hypertension, leg ulcers, priapism, and possibly stroke. Free hemoglobin scavenges **nitric oxide (NO)**, and red cells release arginase, which consumes the arginine needed to make NO. Losing NO causes vasoconstriction and endothelial dysfunction.

Key acute events:
- **VOC**: ischemic pain from microvascular occlusion. Dactylitis (painful swelling of the hands and feet) is often the first sign in infants.
- **Acute chest syndrome**: triggered by infection, fat embolism from infarcted marrow, or hypoventilation after rib pain. It often develops during a pain admission, which is why incentive spirometry is used.
- **Splenic sequestration** and **aplastic crisis**: in an aplastic crisis, **parvovirus B19** infects erythroid progenitors and halts red cell production. The clue is a very low **reticulocyte count**, whereas sequestration shows reticulocytosis and an enlarging spleen.
- **Stroke**: about 11% of children with HbSS had a stroke by age 20 before screening existed. It results from large-vessel vasculopathy of the distal internal carotid and middle cerebral arteries.

Chronic organ damage:
- **Kidney**: the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic, and hypertonic, which promotes sickling. This causes **hyposthenuria** (inability to concentrate urine), papillary necrosis, and later albuminuria.
- **Bone**: avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
- **Eye**: proliferative retinopathy, more common in HbSC.
- **Brain**: silent cerebral infarcts and cognitive effects.

**Hydroxyurea** raises fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which does not join HbS polymers. It reduces pain crises and ACS.
levels.phd:
The pathophysiology goes well beyond simple mechanical plugging. Vaso-occlusion is a multicellular, inflammatory process:
- Sickle reticulocytes express **VLA-4** and **CD36**, which bind VCAM-1 and thrombospondin on activated endothelium.
- **Phosphatidylserine** exposed on damaged red cells promotes adhesion and thrombin generation.
- Neutrophils roll along **P-selectin** and **E-selectin**, adhere, and then capture red cells. Intravital microscopy in sickle mice (Frenette and colleagues) showed this two-step mechanism.
- Heme acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern. It activates **TLR4** and triggers neutrophil extracellular traps. These mechanisms help explain acute chest syndrome in models.

**Polymerization kinetics** link these cellular events to clinical outcomes. Eaton and Hofrichter showed that HbS gelation has a delay time that scales inversely with roughly the 30th power of HbS concentration. If the delay exceeds the time a cell spends in the capillaries, most cells escape before sickling. Dehydration, which raises intracellular hemoglobin concentration through the Gardos channel and KCl cotransport, shortens the delay dramatically. HbF and coinherited alpha-thalassemia lengthen it.

The **hemolysis-endothelial dysfunction** model (Kato, Gladwin) proposed that NO depletion drives pulmonary hypertension, priapism, and leg ulcers. It is controversial. Critics argued that the NO-scavenging effect of plasma hemoglobin is too small. Inhaled NO and sildenafil trials were also disappointing, and sildenafil increased pain episodes.

**STOP trial (1998)**: children with TCD time-averaged mean velocity of at least 200 cm/s who received chronic transfusion had about a 90% reduction in stroke. **STOP II** showed that stopping transfusion led to reversion to high velocities and strokes. **SIT trial** (2014): transfusion also reduced recurrence of silent infarcts. **TWiTCH** (2016) found that hydroxyurea was noninferior to transfusion for maintaining TCD velocities after initial transfusion in children without severe vasculopathy.

**Coinheritance effects** shape disease: alpha-thalassemia lowers stroke risk and hemolysis but may raise avascular necrosis risk, consistent with the higher viscosity of the vaso-occlusive phenotype.
levels.expert:
Clinical pitfalls in acute care:
- **Undertreated pain** remains the dominant failure. Patients often wait far longer for analgesia than patients with similar pain from other conditions, reflecting stigma. Guidelines (ASH 2020) recommend rapid assessment and individualized plans. VOC has no reliable lab marker, so the patient's report guides care.
- **ACS mimics pneumonia**. Patients should receive antibiotics that cover atypical organisms, oxygen, and incentive spirometry. Worsening hypoxemia or multilobar disease calls for transfusion, and exchange transfusion for severe cases.
- **Simple transfusion with hemoglobin well above baseline** raises viscosity and can provoke occlusion. Exchange transfusion lowers HbS percentage without that rise.
- **Hyperhemolysis**: a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction in which the patient's own red cells are destroyed too, so hemoglobin falls below the pre-transfusion level. Alloimmunization is common because donors and recipients differ in red cell antigens. **Extended matching for Rh (C, E) and Kell** reduces it.
- **Acute stroke** in a child calls for urgent exchange transfusion. Adults also develop hemorrhagic stroke and moyamoya collaterals, which neurosurgeons may revascularize with indirect bypass procedures (for example EDAS).

Chronic care and mortality:
- Median survival in high-income settings is still only about the 40s to 50s. Deaths shift toward chronic organ failure, especially kidney disease, pulmonary hypertension (a tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity of at least 2.5 m/s on echo is associated with higher mortality), and sudden death.
- Most deaths globally occur in sub-Saharan Africa, where newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis, and pneumococcal vaccination remain incomplete. **REACH** showed hydroxyurea is safe and effective in African children.

Therapies and open questions:
- **Crizanlizumab** (anti-P-selectin) won approval after SUSTAIN, but STAND failed to confirm its benefit. **Voxelotor**, which raises hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, was withdrawn in 2024 over excess deaths and VOC in later data. This shows that raising hemoglobin is not the same as improving outcomes.
- **L-glutamine** reduces crises modestly.
- Gene therapies such as **exa-cel** (CRISPR editing of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer) and **lovo-cel** largely eliminate VOC. Whether they halt established vasculopathy and organ damage is unknown. Lovo-cel also carries a boxed warning about blood cancers.
- Open question: can treatment prevent silent infarcts and neurocognitive decline in adults?

keyPoints: Complications stem from vaso-occlusion plus chronic hemolysis
Vaso-occlusive pain crisis is the most common reason for hospital visits
Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death and needs urgent care
Transcranial Doppler screening plus transfusion prevents most childhood strokes
Parvovirus B19 causes aplastic crisis with a very low reticulocyte count
Hydroxyurea raises HbF; some gene therapies (exa-cel) target BCL11A to do the same

test.q: Which two processes underlie most sickle cell complications?
test.explain: Sickled cells block small vessels and break apart early. Together these two processes explain most acute and chronic complications.

test.q: Acute chest syndrome is defined as a new lung infiltrate plus:
choices: Painful swelling of the hands and feet
A rapidly enlarging spleen with anemia
test.explain: ACS combines a new infiltrate on chest X-ray with fever or respiratory symptoms such as cough, chest pain, or hypoxemia.

test.q: Which screening test identifies children with sickle cell disease at high stroke risk?
test.explain: TCD ultrasound detects high blood velocity in narrowed brain arteries. Velocity of at least 200 cm/s marked high risk in the STOP trial.

test.q: A child with sickle cell disease has a sudden hemoglobin drop and a very low reticulocyte count. The likely cause is:
test.explain: Parvovirus B19 halts red cell production, causing aplastic crisis. Sequestration would instead show high reticulocytes and a large spleen.

test.q: Why are children with sickle cell disease vulnerable to pneumococcal infection?
choices: Their spleen is damaged by infarction
Their bone marrow stops producing antibodies
Their lungs fill with sickled cells
test.explain: Repeated splenic infarction causes functional asplenia (autosplenectomy). Without a working spleen, encapsulated bacteria are cleared poorly.

test.q: How does hydroxyurea reduce sickling complications?
choices: It enlarges the spleen to filter cells
It removes iron from red cells
It thins the blood like an anticoagulant
test.explain: HbF does not join HbS polymers, so raising it slows polymerization. This reduces pain crises and acute chest syndrome.

test.q: Free hemoglobin from hemolysis promotes vasoconstriction by consuming:
test.explain: Plasma hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, a vasodilator. This contributes to the hemolytic phenotype, which includes pulmonary hypertension.

test.q: Why does the renal medulla favor sickling?
choices: It has high blood flow and high pH
It is cool and well oxygenated
It contains many fetal red cells
It is hypoxic, acidic, and hypertonic
test.explain: Low oxygen, acidity, and high osmolality all promote HbS polymerization. Sickling there impairs urine concentration (hyposthenuria).

test.q: Avascular necrosis in sickle cell disease most classically affects the:
test.explain: The femoral head has a vulnerable blood supply, so vaso-occlusion there leads to bone death.

test.q: A pain crisis caused by blocked small vessels is called a vaso-___ crisis.
test.explain: A vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC) is ischemic pain from microvascular blockage.

test.q: What term describes the spleen being destroyed by repeated infarction in sickle cell disease?
test.explain: Repeated infarction scars and shrinks the spleen, leaving functional asplenia.

test.q: What is the term for painful swelling of the hands and feet, often the first sign of sickle cell disease in infants?
test.explain: Dactylitis results from vaso-occlusion in the small bones of the hands and feet.

kidTest.q: What shape can sickle cells become?
kidTest.explain: Sickle cells bend into a curved shape, like a farmer's sickle.

kidTest.q: Why do sickle cells cause blockages?
choices: They are too small to see
kidTest.explain: Stiff, sticky cells get stuck in tiny blood tubes, like a traffic jam.

kidTest.q: What does a pain crisis feel like?
choices: A mild itch on the skin
kidTest.explain: When blood can't get through, the body part lacks oxygen and hurts a lot.

kidTest.q: Which organ in the belly acts as a blood filter?
kidTest.explain: The spleen filters blood, and sickle cells can get stuck there.

kidTest.q: Doctors use a sound scan to keep this organ safe: b _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: A special sound scan of the head finds brain blood vessels that might get blocked.

advancedTest.q: Why does dehydration of sickle red cells dramatically worsen vaso-occlusion?
choices: It lowers HbS concentration and slows nitric oxide release in vessels
It raises HbS concentration, steeply shortening the polymerization delay time
It raises HbF synthesis, which then co-polymerizes with HbS chains
It activates P-selectin directly on the red cell membrane surface
advancedTest.explain: The delay time scales with roughly the 30th power of HbS concentration, so small rises in concentration make cells sickle before leaving the capillaries.

advancedTest.q: A patient with HbSS and coinherited alpha-thalassemia would be expected to show:
choices: Lower blood viscosity and more frequent leg ulcers
More hemolysis and a clearly higher stroke risk
Less hemolysis, possibly more avascular necrosis
Higher HbF levels and fewer vaso-occlusive events
advancedTest.explain: Alpha-thalassemia reduces hemolysis and stroke risk but raises hemoglobin and viscosity, favoring the vaso-occlusive phenotype, including avascular necrosis.

advancedTest.q: The withdrawal of voxelotor despite its raising of hemoglobin best illustrates that:
choices: Raising oxygen affinity directly reverses sickle vasculopathy
Anti-adhesion drugs outperform agents targeting polymerization
Gene therapy has made disease-modifying drugs obsolete
Raising hemoglobin is a surrogate that may not predict clinical benefit
advancedTest.explain: Hemoglobin rose, but later data showed excess deaths and VOC. Surrogate lab improvements do not guarantee better outcomes.

advancedTest.q: Two weeks after transfusion, a patient's hemoglobin falls below its pre-transfusion level. This most suggests:
choices: Splenic sequestration of the transfused donor cells
Hyperhemolysis of the patient's own red cells
Acute chest syndrome causing hemodilution of blood
Aplastic crisis caused by parvovirus B19 infection
advancedTest.explain: In hyperhemolysis, both donor and patient red cells are destroyed, so hemoglobin drops below baseline, not just back to it.

lessons.title: Thalassemias: Alpha vs Beta Globin Imbalance

levels.kid:
Inside your red blood cells is a special protein called **hemoglobin**. It carries oxygen around your body, like tiny delivery trucks.

Each hemoglobin is built from four pieces. Two pieces are called **alpha** and two are called **beta**. They have to be made in equal amounts, like matching pairs of shoes.

In **thalassemia**, the body makes too few of one kind of piece. Then the leftover pieces have no partner. They clump up and damage the red cells. The cells come out small and pale, and many break early.

Some people with thalassemia feel fine. Others get very tired and need new blood from donors. Thalassemia is passed down in families, the way eye color is.
levels.hs:
**Hemoglobin** in adults is mostly **HbA**, made of two **alpha globin** chains and two **beta globin** chains, each holding a heme group that binds oxygen. Normally the body makes alpha and beta chains in balanced amounts.

**Thalassemias** are inherited conditions in which a person makes too little of one globin chain:
- **Alpha thalassemia**: too few alpha chains. Humans have four alpha globin genes (two on each chromosome 16), and the disease gets worse the more genes are missing.
- **Beta thalassemia**: too few beta chains, usually from point mutations in the single beta globin gene on each chromosome 11.

The real damage comes from the **imbalance**. Unpaired chains clump inside developing red cells. The marrow destroys many of these cells before they mature, which is called **ineffective erythropoiesis**, and the survivors are small (**microcytic**) and pale (**hypochromic**).

Example: a child with **beta thalassemia major** (Cooley anemia) looks healthy at birth because babies still make fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2gamma2). Around 6 to 24 months, as HbF production falls, severe anemia appears. Without treatment the overworked marrow expands and the bones of the face and skull thicken, and the spleen enlarges.

Carriers ("trait") usually have mild or no anemia. Thalassemia is common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian, Southeast Asian and African populations, partly because carriers were protected against malaria.
levels.college:
Adult hemoglobin is about 97% HbA (α2β2), about 2-3% HbA2 (α2δ2) and under 1% HbF (α2γ2). Thalassemias are quantitative defects of globin synthesis. Sickle cell disease is different: it is a qualitative defect, a structurally abnormal beta chain.

**Alpha thalassemia** (genes HBA1/HBA2, chromosome 16) is usually caused by **gene deletions**. Severity tracks the number of the four genes lost:
- 1 deleted: silent carrier, normal blood counts.
- 2 deleted: alpha thal trait, mild microcytosis. The **cis** form (--/αα) is common in Southeast Asia. The **trans** form (-α/-α) is common in people of African descent.
- 3 deleted: **HbH disease**. Excess β chains form β4 tetramers (HbH), which precipitate and cause hemolysis.
- 4 deleted: **Hb Bart's** (γ4) **hydrops fetalis**. Hb Bart's binds oxygen so tightly that it hardly releases any, so the condition is usually fatal before or shortly after birth without intrauterine transfusion.

**Beta thalassemia** (HBB, chromosome 11) usually comes from **point mutations** affecting splicing, the promoter or translation. Alleles are β0 (no output) or β+ (reduced output).
- Trait (minor): microcytosis with **raised HbA2** (above about 3.5%).
- Major: transfusion-dependent from infancy.
- Intermedia: in between.

**Pathophysiology.** Free α chains are highly unstable. They precipitate, generate reactive oxygen species and damage membranes, which kills erythroblasts in the marrow. The anemia raises **erythropoietin**, which drives marrow expansion, extramedullary hematopoiesis and splenomegaly. The ineffective erythropoiesis also suppresses **hepcidin**, so the gut absorbs more iron and overload develops even without transfusion.

**Lab clues.** Thalassemia trait causes marked microcytosis with a near-normal or high RBC count. The **Mentzer index** (MCV/RBC) is often below 13, whereas iron deficiency usually gives a value above 13. Ferritin is normal, and target cells appear on the smear.
levels.phd:
The globin loci are developmentally regulated clusters. The α-like cluster on 16p13.3 (ζ, then α2, α1) is controlled by an upstream enhancer, **MCS-R2 (HS-40)**. The β-like cluster on 11p15.4 (ε, Gγ, Aγ, δ, β) is controlled by the **locus control region (LCR)**. The fetal-to-adult switch depends heavily on **BCL11A**, which represses γ-globin, and on LRF/ZBTB7A.

**Chain imbalance as proteotoxicity.** In β-thalassemia, free α chains cannot form stable homotetramers. They are partly buffered by the chaperone **AHSP** (alpha-hemoglobin stabilizing protein) and cleared by autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Once these buffers are saturated, α-chain hemichromes bind band 3 and protein 4.1, oxidize the membrane and expose phosphatidylserine. The result is apoptosis of late erythroblasts, which is ineffective erythropoiesis. Excess β chains in α-thalassemia form soluble HbH, so the main damage falls on circulating cells as hemolysis rather than on marrow precursors. This is why HbH disease is generally milder than β-thalassemia major with a similar degree of chain deficit.

**Genetic modifiers** explain why patients with the same β genotype can look very different:
- Coinheriting α-thalassemia reduces the free α excess and makes β-thalassemia milder.
- Extra α genes (ααα triplication) worsen β-thalassemia trait.
- Variants that raise HbF ease disease by soaking up α chains as α2γ2. Examples are the BCL11A erythroid enhancer, HBS1L-MYB and the XmnI-Gγ site.

**HbE/β-thalassemia** is very common in Southeast Asia. HbE (β26 Glu→Lys) creates a cryptic splice site, so it behaves as a mild β+ allele.

**Iron dysregulation.** Expanded erythroblasts secrete **erythroferrone (ERFE)**, which suppresses hepcidin. Low hepcidin means ferroportin stays active, raising dietary iron absorption. Non-transferrin-bound iron then enters the heart, liver and endocrine organs through calcium channels and ZIP14.

**Malaria selection.** Haldane proposed in 1949 that thalassemia was common because carriers resisted malaria. Later studies in Papua New Guinea and Africa confirmed that α+-thalassemia protects against severe *P. falciparum* malaria. In Kenya, the combination of α-thalassemia with sickle trait loses this protection (negative epistasis).
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis pitfalls.**
- Iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask β-thalassemia trait. Repeat the HbA2 measurement after iron is replaced.
- α-thalassemia trait has normal HbA2 and a normal electrophoresis in adults. It needs DNA testing such as gap-PCR or MLPA, or the diagnosis is made by excluding other causes.
- δ-globin variants and HbE can confuse HPLC results.
- Premarital and antenatal screening programs pair carrier screening with prenatal diagnosis. Cyprus and Sardinia are classic examples, and they cut births with thalassemia major dramatically. Cell-free fetal DNA testing is emerging.

**Clinical classification** now uses **transfusion-dependent (TDT)** versus **non-transfusion-dependent (NTDT)** thalassemia, rather than genotype labels. NTDT carries a high risk of thrombosis (partly from phosphatidylserine-exposed cells and splenectomy), pulmonary hypertension, extramedullary hematopoietic masses (which can compress the spinal cord) and occult iron overload.

**Monitoring iron.** Ferritin underestimates loading in NTDT. **MRI T2*** measures cardiac and liver iron, and a cardiac T2* below 10 ms predicts heart failure. Iron cardiomyopathy was historically the leading cause of death. Chelation uses deferoxamine, deferasirox or deferiprone, often in combination. Deferiprone requires monitoring for agranulocytosis.

**Disease-modifying therapy.**
- **Luspatercept** is an activin receptor ligand trap that relieves the late-stage block in red cell maturation and reduces transfusion burden.
- **Mitapivat** is a pyruvate kinase activator that has shown benefit in both α- and β-thalassemia.
- **Allogeneic HSCT** from a matched sibling is curative and works best in young patients with good iron control.
- **Gene therapy:** betibeglogene autotemcel (Zynteglo) adds a lentiviral βA-T87Q gene. Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) uses CRISPR to disrupt the BCL11A erythroid enhancer, reactivating HbF. It was approved in 2023-24 and achieved transfusion independence in most trial participants. The open problems are myeloablative busulfan conditioning (infertility, toxicity), cost and access in high-prevalence low-income countries.
- **α-thalassemia major** survival is improving with in-utero transfusion. Trials are also exploring in-utero stem cell transplantation.

**Open questions** include durable HbF induction with oral agents, safer gentler conditioning (antibody-based approaches), and whether hepcidin mimetics or ferroportin inhibitors can correct iron dysregulation and ineffective erythropoiesis together.

keyPoints: Thalassemias are quantitative defects: too little alpha or beta globin is made
Unpaired excess chains precipitate and kill red cell precursors (ineffective erythropoiesis)
Alpha thal is usually gene deletions; severity tracks how many of 4 genes are lost
Beta thal is usually point mutations; trait shows raised HbA2
Low hepcidin and transfusions cause iron overload, monitored with MRI T2*
Cures: stem cell transplant and gene therapies like CRISPR-based HbF reactivation

test.q: What is the basic defect in a thalassemia?
choices: Reduced production of one globin chain
Antibodies directed at red cell membranes
Absence of iron within the heme group
A globin chain with a changed shape
test.explain: Thalassemias are quantitative defects in globin synthesis. A structurally abnormal chain, as in sickle cell disease, is a qualitative defect.

test.q: Most cases of alpha thalassemia are caused by:
test.explain: Alpha thalassemia is usually caused by deletion of one or more of the four alpha globin genes. Beta thalassemia is usually caused by point mutations.

test.q: A person with three of four alpha genes deleted has:
test.explain: Losing three alpha genes leaves excess beta chains, which form beta4 tetramers called HbH.

test.q: Why does beta thalassemia major usually appear between 6 and 24 months of age?
choices: Maternal antibodies wear off by then
test.explain: HbF (alpha2gamma2) needs no beta chains. Symptoms appear as HbF production declines after birth.

test.q: Which lab finding is typical of beta thalassemia trait?
test.explain: HbA2 above about 3.5% suggests beta thal trait. Ferritin is normal and the red cells are small.

test.q: Ineffective erythropoiesis means:
choices: Marrow is replaced by fibrous scar tissue
Red cells are destroyed in the spleen after release
Precursors die in the marrow before they mature
The kidney makes too little erythropoietin
test.explain: Precipitated unpaired chains kill developing erythroblasts inside the marrow.

test.q: Why can thalassemia patients develop iron overload even without transfusions?
choices: Low hepcidin increases gut iron absorption
Their red cells store extra ferritin
test.explain: Ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin, so the gut absorbs more iron.

test.q: A Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) below 13 favors:
test.explain: Thalassemia trait gives marked microcytosis with a preserved red cell count, so the index is low. Iron deficiency usually gives values above 13.

test.q: Why are thalassemia genes common in Mediterranean, African and Asian populations?
choices: Diets there are very low in iron
test.explain: Malaria selected for carriers, as Haldane proposed and later field studies confirmed.

test.q: Four deleted alpha genes cause Hb Bart's ___ fetalis.
test.explain: Hb Bart's (gamma4) binds oxygen so tightly that it hardly releases any, causing fetal hydrops.

test.q: On which chromosome is the beta globin gene located?
test.explain: HBB is on chromosome 11. The alpha genes are on chromosome 16.

test.q: Thalassemic red cells are small and pale, described as microcytic and ___.
test.explain: Less hemoglobin per cell makes the cells pale, which is called hypochromic.

kidTest.q: What does hemoglobin do?
kidTest.explain: Hemoglobin carries oxygen around your body.

kidTest.q: What goes wrong in thalassemia?
choices: Too much water in the blood
Too few of one hemoglobin piece
kidTest.explain: The alpha and beta pieces stop matching because one kind is made in too small an amount.

kidTest.q: How do people get thalassemia?
choices: It is passed down in families
kidTest.explain: It is inherited, like eye color.

kidTest.q: What can help a person with severe thalassemia?
kidTest.explain: Donated blood replaces the missing healthy red cells.

kidTest.q: The two kinds of hemoglobin pieces are alpha and b _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Hemoglobin has two alpha and two beta pieces.

advancedTest.q: Why is HbH disease generally milder than beta thalassemia major with a similar chain deficit?
choices: Excess beta chains form soluble tetramers instead of precipitating in precursors
Hepcidin stays high in alpha thalassemia, which prevents iron loading
HbH releases oxygen more readily than HbA does
Alpha genes are duplicated, so some output survives most deletions
advancedTest.explain: Beta4 tetramers are relatively soluble, so the damage falls mainly on circulating cells. Free alpha chains precipitate in erythroblasts and cause severe ineffective erythropoiesis.

advancedTest.q: A beta thalassemia major genotype causes unexpectedly mild disease. Which coinherited trait best explains this?
advancedTest.explain: Fewer alpha chains reduces the free alpha excess. An alpha triplication would worsen the imbalance.

advancedTest.q: A microcytic patient has borderline HbA2 and low ferritin. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Alpha thalassemia trait is confirmed by the HbA2 level
Beta thalassemia trait is excluded by the HbA2 result
HbE disease is the most likely underlying diagnosis
Low iron may mask beta trait; retest once repleted
advancedTest.explain: Iron deficiency lowers HbA2, so beta trait can be hidden until iron stores are restored. A normal or borderline HbA2 does not confirm alpha trait, which needs DNA testing.

advancedTest.q: Exagamglogene autotemcel helps beta thalassemia mainly by:
choices: Relieving the late erythroid maturation block
Reactivating gamma globin to pair with alpha
Adding a working beta globin gene
advancedTest.explain: Disrupting the BCL11A enhancer raises HbF, which absorbs excess alpha chains. Gene addition describes betibeglogene, and relieving the maturation block describes luspatercept.

lessons.title: Aplastic Anemia & Inherited Marrow Failure Syndromes

levels.kid:
Deep inside your bones is soft stuff called **marrow**. It is like a busy bakery that makes all your blood cells every day: red cells that carry oxygen, white cells that fight germs, and platelets that plug cuts.

In **aplastic anemia**, the bakery almost stops working. The ovens go quiet, and very few new cells come out. So the person feels tired, gets sick easily, and bruises or bleeds more.

Often the body's own guards, the immune cells, attack the bakery by mistake. Some children are born with bakeries that wear out early.

Doctors can calm the guards with medicines. Or they can give a whole new bakery from a donor. That is called a **stem cell transplant**.
levels.hs:
**Bone marrow failure** means the marrow stops making enough blood cells. In **aplastic anemia**, the marrow becomes "empty": the blood-forming tissue is replaced mostly by fat. Because one shared parent cell, the **hematopoietic stem cell**, makes every blood cell type, losing stem cells lowers all three blood cell lines at once. This is called **pancytopenia**:
- Low red cells (anemia): tiredness, paleness, shortness of breath
- Low white cells, especially **neutrophils**: serious infections
- Low platelets: bruising, nosebleeds, tiny red skin dots called petechiae

Most **acquired** aplastic anemia is **autoimmune**: the patient's own **T cells** attack and destroy stem cells. It can also follow certain drugs, toxins like benzene, radiation, or hepatitis.

Some people are born with an **inherited marrow failure syndrome**. The best known is **Fanconi anemia**, where cells cannot properly repair a specific type of DNA damage. Children may have short height, thumb or forearm differences, and a high risk of leukemia.

Doctors confirm the diagnosis with a **bone marrow biopsy**, which shows the empty, fatty marrow. Treatment is either medicines that suppress the immune attack or a **stem cell transplant** that replaces the marrow entirely. Example: a teenager with a fresh case and a matched sibling donor is usually offered transplant, which can cure the disease.
levels.college:
Aplastic anemia (AA) is defined by **pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow** and no abnormal infiltrate or fibrosis. The Camitta criteria grade severity: **severe AA** requires marrow cellularity under 25% plus at least two of neutrophils <0.5 x10^9/L, platelets <20 x10^9/L, and reticulocytes <60 x10^9/L. **Very severe AA** adds neutrophils <0.2 x10^9/L, which brings the highest risk of infection.

**Mechanisms of acquired AA**
- **Immune destruction** (most cases): oligoclonal cytotoxic CD8+ T cells release **interferon-gamma** and **TNF-alpha**, which drive stem cell apoptosis via Fas.
- Direct injury: chemotherapy, radiation, benzene, and idiosyncratic drug reactions (chloramphenicol is the classic example).
- **Hepatitis-associated AA**: appears weeks after a seronegative hepatitis, usually in young males.
- Pregnancy and some viruses (EBV, HIV); parvovirus B19 instead causes pure red cell aplasia.

**Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS)**
- **Fanconi anemia**: defective FANC/BRCA DNA repair pathway; diagnosed by chromosome breakage with diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C.
- **Dyskeratosis congenita / telomere biology disorders**: short telomeres; triad of nail dystrophy, lacy skin pigmentation, oral leukoplakia.
- **Diamond-Blackfan anemia**: ribosomal protein genes (e.g., RPS19); red cells only, with macrocytosis.
- **Shwachman-Diamond syndrome**: SBDS gene; neutropenia plus exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

**Treatment**
- Supportive care: irradiated, leukoreduced blood products and infection prophylaxis.
- **Allogeneic HSCT**: first-line for young patients with a matched sibling donor.
- **Immunosuppressive therapy (IST)**: horse antithymocyte globulin plus cyclosporine, now combined with **eltrombopag**, a thrombopoietin-receptor agonist.

Always screen for an IBMFS before choosing therapy. IST fails in these disorders, and standard transplant conditioning can be toxic in Fanconi anemia.
levels.phd:
Acquired AA is a model of T-cell-mediated organ-specific destruction. Patients show expanded, oligoclonal CD8+ effector clones with skewed TCR Vβ usage, and Treg numbers are reduced. The strongest genetic clue is **HLA class I loss**. Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity of 6p (6pLOH) or inactivating mutations in specific HLA alleles (e.g., HLA-B*40:02) occur in a meaningful fraction of patients. These lesions suggest that stem cells escape by deleting the very antigen-presenting molecules the T cells recognize, which implies a still-unidentified autoantigen.

**Clonal hematopoiesis** is common. Yoshizato et al. (NEJM 2015) sequenced 439 AA patients and found somatic mutations in about one-third. **PIGA**, **BCOR/BCORL1**, and HLA mutations predicted good IST responses and stable courses. **DNMT3A** and **ASXL1** clones tended to expand and were linked to worse outcomes and progression to MDS/AML. AA thus sits on a spectrum with hypoplastic MDS and PNH, and many patients carry small GPI-deficient (PNH) clones that are themselves immune-escape variants.

The IBMFS reveal how genome maintenance governs stem cell fitness. In **Fanconi anemia**, more than 22 FANC genes act in one pathway. The FA core complex monoubiquitinates FANCD2-FANCI at stalled forks to coordinate **interstrand crosslink repair**. Downstream genes include BRCA2 (FANCD1) and PALB2. Aldehydes, both endogenous and from alcohol metabolism, are key crosslink sources. Garaycoechea et al. showed that mice lacking both Aldh2 and Fancd2 develop spontaneous marrow failure, linking ALDH2 variants to accelerated disease in patients.

**Telomere biology disorders** arise from mutations in DKC1, TERT, TERC, TINF2 and related genes. These disorders show genetic anticipation, and telomere length is measured by flow-FISH. In **Diamond-Blackfan anemia**, ribosomal haploinsufficiency causes nucleolar stress. Free ribosomal proteins then bind MDM2, which stabilizes **p53** and triggers erythroid apoptosis. GATA1 translation is also selectively impaired.

Some IBMFS correct themselves through **somatic genetic rescue**. Examples include reversion mosaicism in FA and SAMD9/9L monosomy-7 loss in germline SAMD9L disease. Rescue can be benign or leukemogenic.
levels.expert:
The diagnostic workup is mainly about excluding mimics. These include hypocellular MDS (look for dysplasia, ring sideroblasts, or cytogenetic changes such as monosomy 7), hairy cell leukemia, large granular lymphocyte leukemia, PNH, and anorexia-related gelatinous marrow transformation. Order PNH flow cytometry (FLAER) at baseline and then serially. Screen for an IBMFS in every patient under about 40, and in older patients with suggestive features: chromosome breakage, telomere flow-FISH, and a germline gene panel run on cultured skin fibroblasts. Using fibroblasts avoids somatic reversion artifacts in blood. Telomere disorders often present in adulthood as pulmonary fibrosis, cryptogenic cirrhosis, or a family history of early graying.

**Treatment evidence**
- The RACE trial (Peffault de Latour, NEJM 2022) showed that adding eltrombopag to horse ATG plus cyclosporine raised complete response rates at 3 months without increasing toxicity.
- Horse ATG beat rabbit ATG in a head-to-head study by Scheinberg (NEJM 2011), which was a counterintuitive result.
- Upfront matched-unrelated or haploidentical HSCT (post-transplant cyclophosphamide platforms) is increasingly used in children and young adults, because results now approach those of matched sibling transplants.
- Preferred conditioning is non-myeloablative, and ATG or alemtuzumab is used to limit chronic GVHD. GVHD offers no graft-versus-leukemia benefit in AA, so it is pure harm.

**Pitfalls**
- Transfusing products from a related potential donor can sensitize the patient and promote graft rejection.
- Fanconi patients need reduced-intensity conditioning without radiation, because standard regimens are lethal at their doses.
- Lifelong head-and-neck and anogenital squamous cancer surveillance continues after HSCT in FA, since transplant fixes only the marrow.
- After IST, roughly 10-15% of patients undergo clonal evolution to MDS/AML. Watch for emerging monosomy 7.

**Frontiers**
- Gene therapy: lentiviral FANCA correction (Río et al., Nature Medicine 2019) produced engraftment without conditioning, exploiting the proliferative advantage of corrected cells.
- Danazol: androgen therapy lengthened telomeres in telomere biology disorders (Townsley, NEJM 2016).
- Autoantigen identification in acquired AA remains an open question.
- It is still unclear how to risk-stratify incidental clonal mutations when deciding between IST and transplant.

keyPoints: Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia with an empty, fatty marrow
Most acquired cases are autoimmune: CD8+ T cells destroy stem cells
Fanconi anemia: defective DNA crosslink repair, tested by chromosome breakage
Telomere disorders, Diamond-Blackfan and Shwachman-Diamond are other inherited syndromes
Treatment: stem cell transplant or ATG plus cyclosporine plus eltrombopag
Screen for inherited syndromes and PNH clones before choosing therapy

The spleen traps each cell type

Eating far too much added sugar

lessons.title: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria & Complement Attack

levels.kid:
Your blood has tiny guards called **complement**. They float around and punch holes in germs to destroy them.

But how do guards know not to attack your own cells? Your red blood cells wear little "don't hit me" badges on their outside.

In a rare illness called **PNH**, one blood-making cell in the bone marrow gets a mistake in its instructions. All the red cells it makes are born without their badges. The guards attack them by accident, and the cells burst open.

When red cells burst, the red stuff inside spills into the pee, so it can look dark like cola, often in the morning. People may feel very tired. Doctors now have medicines that calm the guards down, which helps a lot.
levels.hs:
**Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)** is a rare disease in which red blood cells are destroyed by the body's own **complement system**, a group of blood proteins that normally attack bacteria by punching holes in their membranes.

The name describes the classic sign:
- **Paroxysmal**: comes in sudden episodes.
- **Nocturnal**: noticed after sleep (the first morning urine).
- **Hemoglobinuria**: hemoglobin in the urine, making it dark red-brown.

In practice, many patients do not have the night-time pattern, but the name stuck.

The cause is an **acquired mutation** (not inherited) in a gene called **PIGA** in a single blood stem cell. PIGA is needed to build a molecular "anchor" that attaches certain protective proteins to the cell surface. Two of those proteins, **CD55** and **CD59**, normally block complement. Without them, red cells are destroyed inside blood vessels, which is called **intravascular hemolysis**.

PNH causes three main problems:
- **Hemolytic anemia** (tiredness, dark urine).
- **Blood clots**, often in unusual places such as the veins of the liver or brain.
- **Bone marrow failure**, because PNH is closely linked to aplastic anemia.

For example, a young adult with unexplained anemia, dark urine and a clot in the liver veins should be tested for PNH. Doctors diagnose it with **flow cytometry**, which checks whether blood cells are missing these surface proteins.
levels.college:
PNH is an acquired clonal disorder of hematopoietic stem cells. The defect is a somatic mutation in **PIGA**, an X-linked gene encoding a subunit of the enzyme that performs the first step of **glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor** synthesis. Because PIGA is on the X chromosome, a single hit causes complete loss in males and, through X-inactivation, in females too. Every descendant of the mutant stem cell (red cells, granulocytes, monocytes, platelets, lymphocytes) lacks all GPI-anchored proteins.

The two that matter most for hemolysis:
- **CD55 (DAF, decay-accelerating factor)**: speeds breakdown of the C3 and C5 convertases.
- **CD59 (MIRL, membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis)**: blocks C9 from polymerizing into the **membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9)**. Loss of CD59 is the dominant cause of lysis.

Because the **alternative pathway** is always active at a low "tickover" rate, unprotected red cells are lysed continuously, and episodes worsen with infection, surgery or pregnancy.

**Consequences of intravascular hemolysis:**
- Raised **LDH**, low **haptoglobin**, raised reticulocytes, hemoglobinuria and **hemosiderinuria**; the **direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative**, which separates PNH from autoimmune hemolysis.
- Free hemoglobin scavenges **nitric oxide**, causing smooth-muscle dystonia: abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing, erectile dysfunction, fatigue and pulmonary hypertension.
- Chronic urinary iron loss and kidney injury.

**Thrombosis** is the leading historical cause of death, typically at unusual sites: hepatic veins (**Budd-Chiari syndrome**), mesenteric and cerebral venous sinuses.

**Diagnosis:** high-sensitivity **flow cytometry** using **FLAER** (fluorescent aerolysin, which binds the GPI anchor itself) plus antibodies to GPI-anchored markers such as CD24 and CD14 on granulocytes and monocytes, and CD59 on red cells. The older **Ham test** (acidified serum lysis) is obsolete.

**Treatment:** complement inhibition (eculizumab, ravulizumab), and **allogeneic stem cell transplant** as the only cure.
levels.phd:
**Clonal expansion puzzle.** PIGA-null cells have no intrinsic growth advantage; in mouse models they do not outcompete normal cells. Small PNH clones are even detectable in healthy people. The leading explanation is **immune escape**: in aplastic anemia, cytotoxic T cells (possibly CD1d-restricted or NKG2D-mediated, targeting GPI-linked antigens) attack normal stem cells while sparing GPI-deficient ones, letting the PNH clone dominate. This explains why roughly half of aplastic anemia patients carry detectable PNH clones. Additional mutations (e.g., in **HMGA2** or other myeloid genes) can give some clones a true proliferative edge.

**Red cell phenotypes.** Rosse's complement-sensitivity studies defined **type I** (normal), **type II** (partial deficiency, about 3-5x sensitive) and **type III** (complete deficiency, about 15-25x sensitive) red cells. Hemolysis severity tracks the size of the type III population, not the granulocyte clone size.

**Complement biology.** The alternative pathway spontaneously generates C3(H2O); C3b deposits on surfaces and, unchecked, amplifies via factor B and factor D into C3bBb. Normally factor H and CD55 restrain amplification on host cells. CD59 binds C8 and C9 to block MAC pore formation. Inherited isolated CD59 deficiency causes PNH-like hemolysis plus neuropathy, showing CD59 is the key lytic protector.

**Thrombosis mechanisms** are multifactorial and debated: free hemoglobin depleting NO and activating platelets; MAC-induced platelet microparticles exposing phosphatidylserine; loss of GPI-anchored **uPAR** impairing fibrinolysis; tissue factor induction and neutrophil activation. That complement blockade sharply reduces thrombosis supports a central complement role.

**Extravascular hemolysis on C5 blockade.** Blocking C5 stops MAC lysis but leaves upstream C3 activation intact. PNH red cells accumulate **C3d** fragments, becoming DAT-positive for C3, and are cleared by macrophages in the spleen and liver. This residual hemolysis drove development of proximal inhibitors acting at C3 (**pegcetacoplan**), factor B (**iptacopan**) and factor D (**danicopan**).

**Classification:** classic (hemolytic) PNH, PNH in the setting of another marrow failure disorder, and subclinical PNH.
levels.expert:
**Who to test.** Consensus guidance (ICCS/ESCCA flow standards) supports PNH screening in: Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis; aplastic anemia and hypoplastic MDS (screen at diagnosis and periodically); thrombosis at unusual sites, or with cytopenias or hemolysis; and unexplained hemoglobinuria. Testing every routine young venous clot is low-yield.

**Lab pitfalls.**
- Measure clone size on **granulocytes and monocytes**, not red cells. Transfusion dilutes, and hemolysis removes, PNH red cells, so red-cell clones underestimate disease.
- Use FLAER with a lineage gate; single-marker CD55/CD59 panels miss small clones or misread partial (type II) loss.
- Distinguish true breakthrough from extravascular hemolysis: rising LDH suggests intravascular breakthrough; a C3-positive DAT, high reticulocytes and normal-ish LDH point to extravascular clearance.

**Therapy in practice.**
- **Eculizumab** transformed survival toward near-normal. **Ravulizumab** uses engineered neonatal Fc receptor recycling for longer half-life and less frequent infusions. **Crovalimab** is a newer subcutaneous anti-C5 antibody that can work in patients with the **C5 p.Arg885His** variant (common in some East Asian populations), which blocks eculizumab binding.
- **Breakthrough hemolysis** may be pharmacokinetic (drug troughs) or pharmacodynamic (infection or pregnancy driving massive complement activation).
- Proximal inhibitors improve hemoglobin and transfusion independence (pegcetacoplan beat eculizumab in PEGASUS; oral iptacopan showed superiority in APPLY-PNH), but abrupt withdrawal risks severe hemolysis because a large unprotected red-cell pool builds up.
- **Encapsulated bacteria**: terminal complement blockade raises meningococcal risk roughly a thousandfold; vaccination and vigilance are mandatory, and proximal blockade adds pneumococcal and Haemophilus concerns.

**Transplant** is reserved mainly for severe marrow failure, given non-trivial mortality compared with excellent outcomes on drugs.

**Pregnancy** carries high thrombotic and maternal risk; complement inhibition has improved outcomes.

**Open questions:** how best to sequence or combine proximal and terminal inhibitors; whether to treat small clones in aplastic anemia; and a neurosurgical point: in **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** of unclear cause, PNH belongs on the workup.

keyPoints: PNH is an acquired clonal stem cell disorder caused by somatic PIGA mutation
PIGA loss removes GPI-anchored proteins, including complement shields CD55 and CD59
Unprotected red cells are lysed by the membrane attack complex (intravascular hemolysis)
Classic triad: hemolytic anemia, unusual-site thrombosis and marrow failure
Diagnosis is by flow cytometry with FLAER on granulocytes and monocytes; Coombs test is negative
C5 inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) transformed care; proximal inhibitors target extravascular hemolysis

test.q: What is the genetic cause of PNH?
choices: An inherited mutation in the beta-globin gene
An acquired mutation in PIGA in a stem cell
An inherited deletion of alpha-globin genes
An acquired mutation in JAK2 in a stem cell
test.explain: PNH arises from a somatic (acquired) PIGA mutation in one hematopoietic stem cell. Globin mutations cause sickle cell disease and thalassemias.

test.q: Which surface protein loss is the main reason PNH red cells burst?
test.explain: CD59 blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex. Spectrin and band 3 are structural proteins involved in other hemolytic disorders.

test.q: What does the PIGA gene product help build?
test.explain: PIGA is required for the first step of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor synthesis, which tethers CD55 and CD59 to the membrane.

test.q: Where are red cells mainly destroyed in untreated PNH?
choices: In the bone marrow before release
In the liver by Kupffer cells
test.explain: Complement punches holes in red cells directly in the circulation, so hemolysis is intravascular.

test.q: Which result helps separate PNH from autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
test.explain: Untreated PNH is DAT (Coombs) negative because no antibody is involved. High LDH, low haptoglobin and reticulocytosis occur in both conditions.

test.q: A clot in the hepatic veins (Budd-Chiari syndrome) in PNH is an example of:
test.explain: PNH classically causes clots in unusual places such as the hepatic, mesenteric or cerebral veins.

test.q: Why does free hemoglobin cause abdominal pain and trouble swallowing?
choices: It blocks the bile ducts directly
It raises calcium in nerve endings
It scavenges nitric oxide in tissues
test.explain: Free hemoglobin binds nitric oxide, causing smooth-muscle spasm (dystonia) in the gut and blood vessels.

test.q: Which marrow disorder is most closely linked with PNH clones?
test.explain: Around half of aplastic anemia patients carry PNH clones, and the two conditions overlap clinically.

test.q: Eculizumab treats PNH by binding which complement protein?
test.explain: Eculizumab blocks C5, preventing formation of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9).

test.q: What test, using antibodies and FLAER, is used to diagnose PNH?
test.explain: Flow cytometry detects cells missing GPI-anchored proteins.

test.q: The complement pore that lyses cells is called the membrane ___ complex.
test.explain: The membrane attack complex (C5b-9) punches holes in cell membranes.

test.q: What CD-numbered protein, also called decay-accelerating factor, speeds breakdown of complement convertases?
test.explain: CD55 (DAF) dismantles C3 and C5 convertases on the cell surface.

kidTest.q: What does complement normally do?
kidTest.explain: Complement proteins are guards that attack germs.

kidTest.q: In PNH, why do red cells get attacked?
choices: They are too big to move
They have run out of iron
kidTest.explain: Without their protective badges, the guards attack them by mistake.

kidTest.q: What color can pee turn in PNH?
kidTest.explain: Spilled red cell contents make urine dark.

kidTest.q: Where does the mistake in PNH start?
kidTest.explain: One blood-making cell in the bone marrow gets the mistake.

kidTest.q: The guards in your blood are called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Complement is the name for these guard proteins.

advancedTest.q: A PNH patient on eculizumab has normal LDH but persistent anemia, high reticulocytes and a C3-positive DAT. The best explanation is:
choices: Evolution of the clone into acute myeloid leukemia
New warm autoimmune antibodies against red cell antigens
Pharmacokinetic breakthrough with active intravascular lysis
Extravascular clearance of C3-coated PNH red cells
advancedTest.explain: C5 blockade leaves C3 activation intact; C3d-coated cells are cleared by macrophages. Normal LDH argues against intravascular breakthrough.

advancedTest.q: Why should PNH clone size be measured on granulocytes rather than red cells?
choices: Granulocytes carry much more CD59 than red cells
Transfusion and hemolysis shrink the red cell clone
FLAER binds mature red cells better than granulocytes
Red cells lack GPI anchors even in healthy people
advancedTest.explain: Transfusion dilutes and selective destruction removes PNH red cells, so the red cell fraction underestimates the true clone.

advancedTest.q: What best explains why PIGA-null clones expand in aplastic anemia?
choices: PIGA loss gives cells a strong intrinsic growth advantage
Complement lyses normal stem cells but not PNH ones
Immune attack spares GPI-deficient stem cells over normal ones
Transfusions selectively feed the PNH clone with iron
advancedTest.explain: PIGA-null cells lack intrinsic advantage; immune escape from T cells targeting GPI-linked antigens lets them dominate.

advancedTest.q: A patient switched from pegcetacoplan to no therapy abruptly is at special risk because:
choices: Meningococcal vaccine protection is lost on stopping
C5 becomes permanently overactive after C3 blockade
A large unprotected red cell pool can lyse at once
advancedTest.explain: Proximal inhibition lets many unprotected PNH red cells accumulate; removing it can trigger massive hemolysis.
